title: Complete Guide to Zakat
description:
A comprehensive guide to the third pillar of Islam - Zakat. This course covers everything from the basic concept of Zakat to detailed calculations for different types of wealth, distribution methods, and common questions.

Zakat is not merely charity but an obligatory act of worship that purifies wealth and serves the needs of the community. The Quran mentions Zakat alongside prayer over 30 times, emphasizing its integral role in Islam.

This course is designed for beginners and provides practical guidance on how to calculate and pay Zakat correctly. Each lesson includes authentic references from the Quran and Sunnah, as well as classical scholarly opinions on disputed matters.
short_description: Master the calculation, distribution, and spiritual significance of Zakat with authentic references.

modules.title: Understanding Zakat: Concept and Philosophy
modules.description: The spiritual and social significance of Zakat in Islam and its role in society.

lessons.title: The Spiritual Significance of Zakat
lessons.content:
Zakat (obligatory charity) is one of the five pillars of Islam and carries immense spiritual significance. It is not merely a financial transaction but an act of worship that purifies both wealth and soul.

The word 'Zakat' comes from the Arabic root meaning 'purification' and 'growth.' Just as water purifies, Zakat purifies one's wealth from greed, selfishness, and attachment to worldly possessions. Allah (SWT) says: 'Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them increase.' (Quran 9:103)

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Zakat is the right of the poor over the wealth of the rich.' This understanding shifts the perspective from 'giving charity' to 'returning what rightfully belongs to others.' Zakat connects the rich with the poor, creating a bond of brotherhood and mutual responsibility.

Zakat is also a means of spiritual growth and development. By giving away a portion of one's wealth, a Muslim trains their soul to be generous, compassionate, and detached from material possessions. It is a reminder that everything belongs to Allah (SWT) and that humans are merely trustees of what they have been given.

Imam al-Ghazali (رحمه الله) wrote in Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din: 'Zakat purifies the soul from greed and miserliness, and it purifies wealth from decrease and corruption. It is a means of attaining the pleasure of Allah and the success in this world and the Hereafter.'

The spiritual benefits of Zakat include:
1. Purification of wealth from impurities
2. Purification of the soul from greed
3. Increase in blessings (barakah) in remaining wealth
4. Protection from calamities and trials
5. Expiation of sins
6. Drawing closer to Allah (SWT)
7. Preparing for the Day of Judgment

lessons.title: The Social Philosophy of Zakat
lessons.content:
Beyond its spiritual significance, Zakat carries a profound social philosophy that addresses poverty, inequality, and community welfare. It is one of the earliest forms of social security in human history.

Allah (SWT) says: 'Zakat expenditures are only for the poor and for the needy and for those employed to collect [Zakat] and for bringing hearts together [for Islam] and for freeing captives [or slaves] and for those in debt and for the cause of Allah and for the [stranded] traveler. This is an obligation from Allah. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.' (Quran 9:60)

The eight categories of Zakat recipients address various forms of need and hardship in society:
1. Al-Fuqara' (the poor) - those who have little or nothing
2. Al-Masakin (the needy) - those who do not have enough to meet their basic needs
3. Al-Amilina 'Alayha (administrators) - those employed to collect and distribute Zakat
4. Al-Mu'allafatu Qulubuhum (those whose hearts are to be reconciled) - new Muslims or those whose faith needs strengthening
5. Fi al-Riqab (freeing captives or slaves) - assisting in emancipation
6. Al-Gharimin (those in debt) - helping to pay off debts
7. Fi Sabilillah (in the cause of Allah) - general Islamic causes
8. Ibn al-Sabil (the wayfarer) - travelers who are stranded

The social philosophy of Zakat is built on several principles:
1. Wealth redistribution - Zakat takes from the wealthy and gives to the poor, reducing economic inequality.
2. Community solidarity - Zakat creates a bond between the rich and the poor, fostering social cohesion.
3. Economic stimulation - Zakat puts money into the hands of those who need it most, stimulating economic activity.
4. Prevention of hoarding - Zakat discourages hoarding of wealth and encourages its circulation in the economy.
5. Dignity of the poor - Zakat is a right, not a favor, giving the poor dignity and self-respect.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever pays Zakat on his wealth, the Fire will not touch his gold and silver on the Day of Judgment.' (Musnad Ahmad, graded Sahih). This hadith illustrates the protective power of Zakat, both in this world and the Hereafter.

The scholars have emphasized that Zakat is not optional but obligatory. Abu Bakr Siddiq (رضي الله عنه) fought against those who refused to pay it after the death of the Prophet (peace be upon him), saying: 'By Allah, I will fight anyone who differentiates between prayer and Zakat.'

modules.title: Zakatable Wealth and Nisab
modules.description: Understanding what wealth is subject to Zakat and the minimum threshold (Nisab) for obligation.

lessons.title: Nisab: The Minimum Threshold
lessons.content:
Nisab is the minimum amount of wealth that a Muslim must possess for Zakat to become obligatory. It is based on the value of gold and silver as established by the Prophet (peace be upon him).

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no Zakat on less than five awaq of silver or less than five wasaq of dates.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 1485) Five awaq of silver equals approximately 595 grams, and five wasaq of dates equals approximately 613 kilograms.

The Nisab threshold for gold is 85 grams (approximately 2.6 troy ounces), and for silver it is 595 grams (approximately 19 troy ounces). The scholars differ on which Nisab to use for cash:
- The Hanafi school uses the gold Nisab
- The Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali schools use the silver Nisab

The difference is significant: the gold Nisab is approximately $4,500-$5,000 (at current prices), while the silver Nisab is approximately $400-$500. The majority recommend using the lower silver Nisab to ensure more people pay Zakat.

The Nisab for agricultural produce is different: five wasaq of dates or wheat, which equals approximately 613 kilograms.

The Nisab for livestock is also different: five camels, thirty cattle, or forty sheep/goats.

The scholars specify that Zakat becomes obligatory when one possesses the Nisab for one complete lunar year (hawl). If the wealth drops below the Nisab during the year, the hawl restarts. If it remains above the Nisab for a full year, Zakat must be paid on the entire amount.

Imam al-Nawawi (رحمه الله) explained in Al-Majmu': 'The Nisab is determined by the market value of gold or silver at the time of Zakat, not at the time of acquisition. This is to ensure that the Zakat is fair and appropriate.'

It is important to note that Zakat is calculated on the net wealth, meaning that debts should be subtracted from the total wealth before calculating Zakat. For example, if a person has $10,000 in savings but owes $6,000 in debts, the Zakat is calculated on $4,000.

lessons.title: Zakatable Assets: Cash, Gold, and Silver
lessons.content:
Cash, gold, and silver are the most common forms of Zakatable wealth. This lesson covers the detailed rules for each.

Cash:
1. Zakat is payable on all forms of currency, including paper money, coins, and digital currencies.
2. The Nisab for cash is determined by the silver Nisab (approximately $400-$500) for the majority, or the gold Nisab (approximately $4,500-$5,000) for the Hanafi school.
3. Zakat is calculated at 2.5% (1/40th) of the total cash.
4. Cash in savings accounts, checking accounts, and under the mattress is all subject to Zakat.
5. The scholars differ on whether gold and silver coins are considered cash or separate assets; the majority say they are separate assets.

Gold:
1. Zakat is payable on all gold jewelry and bullion, whether worn or stored.
2. The Nisab for gold is 85 grams (approximately 2.6 troy ounces).
3. Zakat is calculated at 2.5% of the total gold value.
4. The scholars differ on whether gold jewelry worn by women is subject to Zakat:
   - The majority (Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) say it is subject to Zakat if it reaches the Nisab.
   - The Hanafi school says it is not subject to Zakat if it is for personal use.
5. Gold in the form of coins, bars, or investment is subject to Zakat regardless of the amount.

Silver:
1. Zakat is payable on all silver jewelry, coins, and bullion.
2. The Nisab for silver is 595 grams (approximately 19 troy ounces).
3. Zakat is calculated at 2.5% of the total silver value.
4. The scholars differ on whether silver jewelry is subject to Zakat, similar to gold jewelry.

The scholars also discuss the ruling on platinum and other precious metals. The majority say that platinum is not subject to Zakat because it was not known during the time of the Prophet (peace be upon him). However, some scholars say it is subject to Zakat if it is considered a form of wealth.

The method of calculation is straightforward: take the total value of cash, gold, and silver, subtract debts, and if the remaining amount reaches the Nisab, pay 2.5% as Zakat.

The scholars emphasize the importance of paying Zakat on time and not delaying it. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Pay the Zakat on your wealth before the day comes when gold and silver are brought to you.' (Musnad Ahmad, graded Hasan)

lessons.title: Zakat on Business Assets and Trade Goods
lessons.content:
Business owners and traders have specific rules regarding Zakat on their assets and trade goods. This lesson covers the detailed rulings.

Zakat on Trade Goods:
1. All items held for sale are subject to Zakat at their current market value, not their purchase price.
2. The scholars differ on what constitutes 'trade goods':
   - The Maliki school says any item intended for sale, regardless of the seller's profession.
   - The Shafi'i and Hanbali schools say items that are regularly sold by the seller.
   - The Hanafi school says items that are sold in the regular course of business.
3. Zakat is calculated at 2.5% of the total value of trade goods at the end of the hawl.
4. If the items are for personal use, they are not subject to Zakat.

Zakat on Business Capital:
1. The capital of a business is subject to Zakat, regardless of the type of business.
2. The scholars differ on whether the business is considered 'trade goods' or 'cash':
   - If the business deals in goods, its inventory is subject to Zakat as trade goods.
   - If the business deals in services, its capital is subject to Zakat as cash.
3. The scholars also discuss the Zakat on the tools and equipment of a business; the majority say they are not subject to Zakat if they are essential for the business.

Zakat on Shares and Stocks:
1. The scholars have discussed the ruling on shares and stocks extensively.
2. The majority say that shares are subject to Zakat at their market value, not their face value.
3. The Zakat is calculated at 2.5% of the total value of the shares.
4. If the company deals in haram (forbidden) products or services, the scholars differ on whether Zakat should be paid on the shares.

Zakat on Real Estate:
1. Personal homes are not subject to Zakat according to the majority.
2. Investment properties (rental properties) are subject to Zakat at their current market value.
3. The scholars differ on whether Zakat should be paid on the rental income or the property itself:
   - The majority say Zakat is paid on the rental income as cash.
   - Some scholars say Zakat should be paid on the property itself as an investment.

The scholars emphasize that business owners should maintain accurate records and calculate Zakat regularly. It is recommended to set aside a portion of profits for Zakat throughout the year to avoid the burden of a large payment at the end of the hawl.

modules.title: Distribution of Zakat
modules.description: Understanding the eight categories of Zakat recipients and how to distribute Zakat correctly.

lessons.title: The Eight Categories of Recipients
lessons.content:
Allah (SWT) has specified eight categories of people who are eligible to receive Zakat. These categories are mentioned in Surah At-Tawbah, and it is not permissible to give Zakat to anyone outside of these categories.

Allah (SWT) says: 'Zakat expenditures are only for the poor and for the needy and for those employed to collect [Zakat] and for bringing hearts together [for Islam] and for freeing captives [or slaves] and for those in debt and for the cause of Allah and for the [stranded] traveler. This is an obligation from Allah. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.' (Quran 9:60)

The eight categories are:

1. Al-Fuqara' (the poor) - those who have little or nothing. They are not able to meet their basic needs. The scholars say that a person is considered poor if they do not have enough for one year's expenses.

2. Al-Masakin (the needy) - those who do not have enough to meet their basic needs. They may have some wealth but it is insufficient. The scholars say that a person is considered needy if they have some wealth but it is less than the Nisab.

3. Al-Amilina 'Alayha (administrators) - those employed to collect and distribute Zakat. The scholars say that these workers are entitled to a portion of the Zakat for their services. The scholars differ on whether this category is still applicable today.

4. Al-Mu'allafatu Qulubuhum (those whose hearts are to be reconciled) - new Muslims or those whose faith needs strengthening. This category was applicable during the time of the Prophet (peace be upon him) when non-Muslims were being invited to Islam. Some scholars say this category is still applicable in certain circumstances.

5. Fi al-Riqab (freeing captives or slaves) - assisting in emancipation. This category was applicable during the time when slavery existed. Some scholars say that this category is still applicable for assisting those in debt or other forms of bondage.

6. Al-Gharimin (those in debt) - helping to pay off debts. The scholars say that this category applies to those who have debts that they cannot pay off, and the debt was not incurred for sinful purposes.

7. Fi Sabilillah (in the cause of Allah) - general Islamic causes, including jihad, da'wah, and community projects. The scholars differ on the scope of this category:
   - The Hanafi school says it includes only jihad.
   - The Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali schools say it includes all general Islamic causes.

8. Ibn al-Sabil (the wayfarer) - travelers who are stranded. The scholars say that this category applies to travelers who are away from home and have insufficient funds to return.

The scholars emphasize that the Zakat should be distributed according to the needs of the community. If one category has more needs, more Zakat should be given to that category. The scholars also say that it is permissible to give Zakat to one person or to divide it among multiple recipients.

lessons.title: Practical Guide to Zakat Distribution
lessons.content:
This lesson provides a practical guide to distributing Zakat correctly, including common scenarios and scholarly opinions.

Common Scenarios:

1. Paying Zakat to family members:
- It is permissible to give Zakat to one's spouse, parents, children, and other relatives.
- The majority say that it is permissible to give Zakat to one's parents, but it is better to give it to others.
- The Hanafi school says it is not permissible to give Zakat to one's parents or grandparents.
- It is not permissible to give Zakat to one's spouse if she is rich (has the Nisab).

2. Paying Zakat to the poor in one's community:
- The scholars recommend giving Zakat to the poor in one's local community first, then to other communities.
- The scholars say that it is permissible to send Zakat to other countries if there is a greater need there.

3. Paying Zakat through organizations:
- It is permissible to give Zakat to organizations that distribute it to the eligible recipients.
- The scholars say that the organization must be trustworthy and ensure that the Zakat reaches the eligible recipients.

4. Paying Zakat on behalf of deceased relatives:
- If a person dies without paying Zakat that was due, it is obligatory for their heirs to pay it from their estate.
- The scholars say that the heirs should pay the Zakat before distributing the inheritance.

5. Paying Zakat on behalf of others:
- It is permissible to pay Zakat on behalf of others, such as family members or community members.
- The scholars say that the person paying must have the intention to pay on behalf of the other person.

Method of Distribution:
1. Calculate the total Zakatable wealth and subtract debts.
2. Determine if the remaining amount reaches the Nisab.
3. Calculate 2.5% of the total.
4. Identify eligible recipients in the eight categories.
5. Distribute the Zakat to the recipients.

The scholars emphasize the importance of distributing Zakat promptly and not delaying it. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Give Zakat before the day comes when gold and silver are brought to you.' (Musnad Ahmad, graded Hasan). This hadith illustrates the urgency of paying Zakat.

It is also important to maintain records of Zakat distribution and to ensure that the Zakat reaches the eligible recipients. The scholars say that the person distributing Zakat will be questioned on the Day of Judgment about how they distributed it.

modules.title: Special Cases and Common Questions
modules.description: Addressing specific situations and frequently asked questions about Zakat calculation and payment.

lessons.title: Zakat al-Fitr: The Zakat of Breaking the Fast
lessons.content:
Zakat al-Fitr is a separate form of Zakat that is obligatory on every Muslim at the end of Ramadan. It is due before the Eid prayer and is intended to purify the fasting person from any shortcomings during Ramadan.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The Zakat al-Fitr is purification (Siyam) for the fasting person from any improper behavior, and food for the poor. If one pays it before the Eid prayer, it is accepted Zakat. If one pays it after the Eid prayer, it is considered charity.' (Sunan Abu Dawud 1609, graded Sahih)

The amount of Zakat al-Fitr is one Sa' (approximately 2.5 kg) of the staple food of the locality. The scholars differ on whether it should be paid in cash or in kind:
- The majority (Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) say it should be paid in kind (food)
- The Hanafi school says it can be paid in cash

The scholars also differ on the amount when paid in cash:
- The Shafi'i school says it should be equivalent to the value of one Sa' of food
- The Hanbali school says it should be equivalent to the value of one Sa' of dates or barley
- The Maliki school says it should be equivalent to the value of one Sa' of the local staple food

Zakat al-Fitr is obligatory on:
1. Every Muslim, regardless of age or gender
2. The head of the household pays for all family members, including children and dependents
3. Those who have the Nisab (according to the majority)

The scholars emphasize that Zakat al-Fitr should be paid before the Eid prayer. The Prophet (peace be upon him) instructed that it be paid before the people go out for Eid prayer. This is to ensure that the poor have enough to celebrate Eid with the rest of the community.

The scholars also discuss the ruling on paying Zakat al-Fitr for non-Muslim family members. The majority say it is not permissible to pay Zakat al-Fitr for non-Muslims, as Zakat is an act of Islamic worship that is specific to Muslims.

Zakat al-Fitr is a means of purifying the fasting person from any shortcomings during Ramadan, such as idle speech or minor sins. It also ensures that the poor have enough to celebrate Eid with the rest of the community, fostering social cohesion and unity.

lessons.title: Common Questions About Zakat
lessons.content:
This lesson addresses the most frequently asked questions about Zakat, with answers based on authentic references.

Q1: Should I pay Zakat on my car or home?
A: No, personal vehicles and homes are not subject to Zakat according to the majority. However, investment properties and vehicles used for business are subject to Zakat.

Q2: Should I pay Zakat on my retirement savings (401k, IRA)?
A: Yes, retirement savings are subject to Zakat. The scholars say that the account should be treated as cash, and 2.5% should be paid on the total value.

Q3: Should I pay Zakat on my stocks and mutual funds?
A: Yes, stocks and mutual funds are subject to Zakat. The scholars say that the Zakat should be calculated on the current market value of the shares, not their face value.

Q4: Should I pay Zakat on the gold jewelry I wear?
A: According to the majority (Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali), gold jewelry is subject to Zakat if it reaches the Nisab. The Hanafi school says it is not subject to Zakat if it is for personal use.

Q5: Should I pay Zakat on my business equipment?
A: No, business equipment that is essential for the business is not subject to Zakat. However, excess equipment that is not being used is subject to Zakat.

Q6: Should I pay Zakat on my debts?
A: No, you do not pay Zakat on debts that you owe. However, if you are the creditor (someone owes you money), you should pay Zakat on the debts if they are expected to be repaid.

Q7: When should I pay Zakat?
A: Zakat is due when your wealth reaches the Nisab and has been in your possession for one complete lunar year (hawl). It is recommended to pay Zakat promptly and not delay it.

Q8: Can I pay Zakat in advance?
A: Yes, it is permissible to pay Zakat in advance. The scholars say that it is better to pay Zakat promptly rather than delay it.

Q9: Should I pay Zakat on my cryptocurrency?
A: The scholars have discussed the ruling on cryptocurrency extensively. The majority say that cryptocurrency is subject to Zakat if it reaches the Nisab. The scholars differ on the method of calculation, but most say it should be treated as a form of wealth.

Q10: Should I pay Zakat on my student loans?
A: No, you do not pay Zakat on debts that you owe, including student loans. However, if you are the creditor (someone owes you money), you should pay Zakat on the debts if they are expected to be repaid.

The scholars emphasize that Zakat is a right of the poor over the wealth of the rich, and it should not be taken lightly. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever pays Zakat on his wealth, the Fire will not touch his gold and silver on the Day of Judgment.' (Musnad Ahmad, graded Sahih)
